intro: Each graded component of the course is scored out of 100 points using the rubric below, and that score is then weighted according to the syllabus. Every criterion is assessed at one of four levels. Excellent work falls in the top tenth of a criterion's points, Proficient in the next tenth, Developing in the next, and Beginning covers anything below.

Read the rubric for an assignment before you submit it. The criteria follow the assignment prompts in the syllabus closely, so the rubric is also a checklist of what each assignment asks you to do. Late penalties (5% per day, including weekends) are applied to the rubric score after grading. Work submitted in violation of the course's academic integrity and AI policies is not scored with the rubric, and is subject to additional processes.

assignments.title: Writing Assignment 1: The EU in the News
assignments.meta: 500 words minimum · Due Friday of Week 5 (9/25) at 11:59pm
assignments.note: Half of this rubric rests on your familiarity with the two institutions you choose, since that is the core of the assignment.

levels.desc: Clearly and accurately explains what is happening, why it matters, and who is involved (governments, EU bodies, parties, interest groups, publics), drawing on the article.
Accurately describes the issue and its main actors, with minor gaps in context or significance, or contains minor issue summary mistakes that do not impede understanding.
Describes the issue in general terms; key actors or context are vague or missing, or has significant issue summary errors that impede understanding.
The issue is unclear or inaccurate, or the article is summarized without identifying who is involved.

criteria.name: Familiarity with institution 1

levels.desc: Shows precise command of the institution's composition, powers, and decision rules from the institutions unit (Weeks 4–5), and uses that knowledge to explain what the institution can and cannot do on this issue.
Accurately describes the institution's role and powers with minor imprecision; the link to the issue is sound but less developed.
Describes the institution in general terms, or confuses some powers or procedures (for example, the European Council with the Council of the EU).
The description is largely inaccurate, missing, or disconnected from course material.

levels.desc: Gives a realistic, specific account of how the two institutions and their political actors would engage the issue, respecting the limits of their competences and showing how they interact. Creative framing, if used, stays grounded in how the EU actually works.

assignments.title: Writing Assignment 2: The Image and the Crisis
assignments.meta: 500 words minimum · Due Saturday of Week 11 (11/7) at 11:59pm
assignments.note: Students who request the alternative prompt are graded on the same criteria, adapted to that prompt.

levels.desc: Identifies the image precisely and explains when, where, and how it circulated, describing it accurately and with care, without gratuitous detail.
Identifies the image and its context accurately, with minor gaps in how or where it circulated.
Context is thin or partly inaccurate; circulation is not explained.
The image or its context is unclear or inaccurate.

Explains the response the image produced and supports it with at least one concrete, sourced outcome (donations, policy statements, media coverage patterns, or public opinion data), with attention to timing.
Cites at least one concrete outcome accurately; explanation of the broader response or its timing is less developed.
Describes the response in general terms; the concrete outcome is vague, unsourced, or loosely connected to the image.
No concrete outcome, or the response is asserted without evidence.

Engages at least two assigned Week 11 readings substantively and represents their findings accurately. Concepts (identifiable victim effect, compassion fade, psychic numbing, the pull of children's faces) are applied to the image, not just named.
Uses two readings accurately; application of the concepts is sound but uneven or partly descriptive.
Readings are cited but concepts are named rather than applied, or only one reading is used meaningfully.
Fewer than two readings, or the readings are misrepresented.
Makes an evidence-based argument for why images like this one move public opinion more than statistics or images of adults, or why the effect faded. The stance is analytical throughout.
The argument is present and mostly analytical, with some reliance on assertion or personal reaction.
The argument is implied rather than made; the piece leans on how the image made the writer feel.
No explanatory argument; the piece is primarily a personal response.
Clear, organized, and carefully proofread; treats the subject seriously and respectfully.
Generally clear, with a few lapses in flow or mechanics.
Organization or frequent errors make parts hard to follow, or tone is occasionally inappropriate to the subject.
Disorganized or difficult to read throughout.

assignments.title: The Empathy Debate
assignments.note: Students with a documented absence on debate day submit a written brief of approximately 500 words for their assigned side. The brief is graded on the first three criteria as written; the fourth becomes the clarity and organization of the brief, and the brief should include a response to the strongest argument on the other side.

criteria.name: Prepared argument grounded in the readings

levels.desc: Arrives with at least one well-developed argument that draws accurately on specific assigned readings from Weeks 10 and 11, including Bloom where relevant.
Prepared argument is sound and draws on the readings, with some imprecision.
Argument is prepared but only loosely connected to the readings.
No evident preparation, or the argument does not use the readings.

criteria.name: From psychology to a normative claim

levels.desc: Converts the psychological findings into a clear normative claim about how policy should or should not respond to empathy, rather than restating the findings.
Makes a normative claim, though the step from evidence to claim is not fully spelled out.
Mostly restates the psychology; the normative claim is thin or implied.
No normative claim.
Responds directly to the strongest opposing arguments and anticipates rebuttals.
Responds to opposing arguments, though sometimes to weaker versions of them.
Engagement is limited or talks past the other side.
No engagement with opposing arguments.
Clear, concise, and within time; respectful toward opponents and collaborative with teammates.
Generally clear and respectful, with minor issues of timing or focus.
Hard to follow at points, or contributes unevenly to the team.
Unclear, disruptive, or disrespectful.

Contributes regularly across all units, including any interactive Fridays.
Contributes in most weeks, with occasional quiet stretches.
Contributes sporadically.

Attends consistently and arrives on time; any absences are communicated.

Repeated absences or tardiness.

Listens, builds on classmates' points, and disagrees respectfully.
Generally respectful and attentive, occasionally talks past others.

Disrespectful or disruptive.

guide.covers: The country's history in the EU; the landmark events and reasons that led to membership; an argued view of its future membership; internal crises or shifts in public opinion, in the country, its neighbors, or the EU, that may threaten stability.

Why the country wants, or may want, to join or not; the benefits and the compromises entry would require, tied to the accession process (Weeks 12–13); relevant historical events in the country's history; geopolitical context. A paper on the United Kingdom must engage the Week 9 material.

guide.option: Option 3: Identity or the migration crisis
guide.covers: Applies the social psychological frameworks from Weeks 7–11 to a specific country, event, or campaign. The readings must do analytical work in the argument, not serve as decoration, and the paper must still show command of EU institutions and processes.
